terms.gloss: shut out, keep out, exclude; rule out
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive; ab + abl., or the abl. alone
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.134: nec vērō … exclūdat aliōs
Quint. 1.1.26: nōn exclūdō, I don’t rule it out
terms.comment: To shut someone out of a place, a talk or a share: Gādītānī Poenōs moenibus exclūsērunt (Cic. Balb. 39; Lewis & Short). It is also the word for a hen hatching chicks (Comenius, after Cicero).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.111: quod verba sint praetermissa (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Leaving out in speaking or writing, or letting a chance go by.
Excluding from a rule or a list: see exception.

phrases.latin: nec vērō, tamquam in possessiōnem suam vēnerit, exclūdat aliōs, sed cum reliquīs in rēbus, tum in sermōne commūnī vicissitūdinem nōn inīquam putet
phrases.english: and he should not shut others out, as if he had come into his own property, but think it fair, in conversation as in everything else, to take turns

phrases.latin: nōn exclūdō autem, id quod est inventum irrītandae ad discendum īnfantiae grātiā, eburneās etiam litterārum fōrmās in lūsum offerre
phrases.english: I don’t rule out the thing invented to tempt small children to learn, giving them ivory letters to play with

sources: Lewis & Short: excludo · Lewis & Short: praetermitto · Lewis & Short: excipio
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-quintilianus), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
